description: We are VEX, an innovative team of students specializing in Software Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, and Data Science. Our skills encompass Python development, similarity algorithms, database management, full-stack web platforms, and IoT integration. We are passionate about leveraging intelligent data matching techniques to bridge Earth's unique geological landscapes—especially in Oman—with planetary environments on the Moon and Mars for future space exploration missions.
summary: Oman Analog Explorer is a free, bilingual (English/Arabic) website that finds where in Oman astronauts and rovers could rehearse Moon and Mars missions. We compare five Omani field sites with Mars landing regions and the lunar south pole using NASA terrain, climate and spectral data, with an open formula, a confidence value and a list of differences for every score. VEX Scout extends this to the whole country: 449 grid cells covering all of Oman are scored, and a virtual drone lets you fly any cell over real NASADEM terrain and satellite imagery. An explainable AI compares each place with 16 established analog sites (such as Desert RATS, MDRS, HI-SEAS and AMADEE-18) and says in plain words why it fits or not. Every flight is saved to a printable mission log. It matters because analog fieldwork is expensive: this tool helps teams screen a whole country from a browser before they send anyone into the desert, and it shows Oman's potential as an analog destination.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Oman Analog Explorer answers one question: where in Oman can teams rehearse Moon and Mars missions, and how sure are we? The site has four connected parts:

1. Explorer and Atlas: five Omani sites (Samail Ophiolite, Umm as Samim, Sharqiya Sands, the Dhofar AMADEE-18 site, Jebel Shams) compared with four Mars targets (Jezero Crater, Nili Fossae, Terra Sirenum chlorides, Nili Patera dunes) and the lunar south pole (Shackleton rim). Users can change the weights of the similarity index and see the score, its confidence and the differences update live.

2. VEX Scout map: all of Oman divided into 449 cells of 0.25 degrees. Each cell has a Mars score, a Moon score, a field-team decision (GO, CONDITIONAL, NO-GO), climate, land cover, flood risk and nearby place names in English and Arabic.

3. VEX Scout drone: a virtual drone that flies over real terrain in any cell, with satellite imagery, 3D buildings, a sun-angle slider for shadows, a chase camera, gamepad support, a mini-map and a cinematic mode. The drone can scan a spot, take photos and drop markers.

4. Mission Log: every flight is saved with its route, distance, photos, markers, landings and the AI explanation, and can be printed as a PDF report or exported as a KML path.

HOW IT WORKS

- A Python pipeline reads NASA data once and writes small JSON files. The website is static (React and TypeScript) and needs no server.

- Terrain is compared on a common 463 m scale (slope, roughness, relief), so 30 m Earth data and 463 m Mars data are not mixed directly.

- The same similarity formula runs in Python and TypeScript, and a parity test fails the build if they ever differ.

- The explainable AI is a k-nearest-neighbour model (k = 3) over six features: slope, roughness, relief, aridity, dry air and day-night temperature swing. It names the three most similar known analog sites and lists which features match and which differ.

- We validated it with leave-one-out: for the Moon, 8 of 10 known analog sites score higher than 90% of Omani cells. For Mars it is weaker (3 of 10), and the site says so.

- Rules and AI are kept separate. When they disagree, the site says "opinions differ, worth a field visit" instead of hiding it.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Screens a whole country from a browser before any expensive field trip.

- Honest by design: every score has a confidence value, its data source and its limits.

- Bilingual English and Arabic, works on desktop, tablet and phone, free and open source.

- We want Oman to be considered as a destination for Moon and Mars analog campaigns, building on the AMADEE-18 Mars simulation held in Dhofar in 2018. The same method can be reused for any country with open NASA data.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Instead of a static map of a few known sites, we turned analog screening into something you can fly: a virtual drone over real NASA elevation data for any place in the country, with an AI that explains its answer in plain words and a mission log like a real field campaign.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: we show confidence, missing data and where the model is weak, rather than only the best numbers.

- Fair comparison: Earth, Mars and Moon data have different resolutions, so we compare them on a common scale.

- Field safety and logistics: slope, flood risk, climate, distance and human footprint decide GO or NO-GO, not similarity alone.

- Accessibility: Arabic and English, no login, and it runs on a phone.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Python (rasterio, xarray, earthaccess, NumPy, pytest, DuckDB), TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Leaflet and react-leaflet, Recharts, WebGL for the 3D drone view, GitHub Actions for data processing, and Vercel for hosting.

USE OF AI TOOLS

The "Why this place?" panel is our own explainable k-nearest-neighbour model, not a generative AI. During development we used Claude (Anthropic) to help write and debug code, interface text and documentation; commits made with its help are marked "Co-Authored-By: Claude" in the Git history. The team chose the idea, the data sources and the design, and reviewed and tested all output. Every number on the site is computed from the cited NASA and partner datasets, not generated by AI.
